book: 032 - Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth

chapters.relation: Kaag reads 'Atlantic City' (Nebraska) as a parable of fatalism: after the Chicken Man bombing in Philadelphia and stuck with 'debts no honest man can pay,' the narrator takes the Coast City bus and finally agrees to 'do a little favor' for a criminal. Following the American philosopher John J. McDermott's philosophy of transience, the refrain 'Everything dies, baby, that's a fact / but maybe someday everything comes back' holds Heidegger's ownmost death together with tentative pragmatic hope. Suburban 'winners' who leave before dark are dead to experience, while the transient, like Camus's indifferent Stranger in 'Nebraska' ('I guess there's just a meanness in this world'), must celebrate meaning in the fleeting qualitative moments of the journey itself.

McKenna and Pratt use McDermott's 'Promethean self' and meliorism to answer the riddle of Nebraska's closer 'Reason to Believe': among the dead dog, the deserted bride and the groom left at the altar, 'still at the end of every hard earned day people find some reason to believe.' They trace Springsteen's shift from escape songs ('Born to Run,' 'Thunder Road') to life at the edge ('Badlands,' 'Darkness on the Edge of Town,' and the two midnight drivers of 'State Trooper' and 'Open All Night'), arguing meaning is made by cutting and connecting relations at the margins. Belief without evidence of salvation is legitimate hope but illegitimate certainty; the reason to believe is Jamesian meliorism — making things 'not perfect, simply better.'

Keith reads 'My Hometown' — whitewashed windows, the textile mill closing, Bruce telling his son 'take a good look around' — through Putnam's Bowling Alone, Dewey's socially constituted self, and Mead, to argue that Bruce and Kate should recommit to their dying town rather than flee in the moving van. Leopold's 'two spiritual dangers in not owning a farm' and Berry's healthy community as ecosystem ground an 'enlightened localism' that avoids both the town's racist parochialism and rootless cosmopolitanism. Volunteering, local food, and town-meeting democracy are the hometown security the song's sadness calls for.

Ventimiglia sets Augustine's three answers to the problem of evil (free will, the toddler-at-the-doctor 'greater good,' evil as privation) against Nebraska's title track, where mass murderer Charlie Starkweather's 'I guess there's just a meanness in this world' makes Augustine's metaphysical gymnastics look like sophistry. 'Atlantic City' and 'Johnny 99' show free will compromised by debts, job loss and winners-and-losers, and Springsteen neither glorifies nor explains evil away. What Bruce and Augustine share is the yearning for redemption: Plato's Symposium pictures Eros — poor, barefoot, homeless, a hunger for the beautiful — and Springsteen answers that hunger with temporary moments of deliverance ('meet me tonight in Atlantic City') rather than guaranteed salvation.

chapters.file: ch25 - Driftin’ Off to a Foreign Land.md
chapters.relation: Dick explains how 'Straight Time' makes us see Charlie's cycle of drudgery through Sartre's The Imaginary: the title is a Sartrean sign that welds prison time, rendering-factory time and straight-and-narrow time into one image of endless oppression, and Bruce's first-person characterization works like Dana Carvey impersonating Jimmy Stewart — consciousness overlooks discrepancies until we recognize 'our' Charlie. Against the escape fantasy of 'Thunder Road,' Camus's Sisyphus frames Charlie as swapping rocks (prison, factory, his uncle's car-theft heist) while the hill remains and 'there is no top of the hill.' Springsteen's answer to the absurd is to climb alongside his characters in empathetic brotherly love.

chapters.file: ch26 - The Final Word That’s Right, I Said Preliminary Thoughts.md
chapters.relation: Patton starts from wildly disputed Springsteen interpretations — Reagan's 1984 campaign use of 'Born in the U.S.A.,' Flint protesters playing 'My Hometown' as civic pride, Kerry's 'No Surrender' — and asks whether any reading is better than another. He frames the issue as Socratic dialectic versus Gorgias-style rhetoric, passes through Augustine's polysemy (multiple intended levels of meaning, as in 'I'm on fire') to Nietzsche's claim that the text disappears beneath its interpretation, extended by Foucault (truth as an instrument of power) and Derridean deconstruction. His conclusion: authorial intent cannot settle meaning, but some readings ('Born in the U.S.A.' as pro-Reagan anthem) are non-starters, otherwise it is rhetoric all the way down and the sophists win.

Calef asks how fictional story-songs can teach: lyrics yield neither know-how nor know-that, since Plato's Theaetetus shows true belief is not knowledge (the 'Meeting Across the River' narrator's plan works only by luck). The answer is a third kind — knowing what something is like: 'The River' lets a comfortable listener inhabit Mary's husband's slide into a dry marriage, and 'Nebraska' lets us feel Starkweather's numb void, 'what it's like to have no soul.' Aristotle's Poetics (we delight in imitation because learning pleases; poetry is more philosophic than history because it speaks in universals) explains why sad songs satisfy us, and Sartre's universal human condition grounds the empathy that makes The Rising render 9/11 ('You're Missing,' 'Empty Sky') thinkable at a personal scale.

The Bells parallel Socrates' forcible 'abduction' to the house of the arms merchant Cephalus in Republic Book I with Springsteen's 1984 political abduction, when Reagan and Mondale both pretended he had endorsed them and George Will invited him to be laureate of 'joyous overconsumption.' They read the Republic's luxurious city — its Ring of Gyges parasites, censorship of poets, and wars born of appetite — as an elenchus run against the control (epoche) of the healthy working city of Book II, so readers who take the 'ideal' city at face value err exactly like fans who hear patriotism in 'Born in the U.S.A.' Songs like 'Youngstown,' 'The Angel' and 'Galveston Bay' likewise critique overconsumption, imperialism and the censorship of artists, and both artist-critics risk the martyrdom Socrates suffered for speaking truth to the powerful.

Auxier's epilogue teaches readers to build playful 'ontologies' from the book's list of Springsteen's proper names — imagining Elvis's .44 Magnum ('Betsy') traveling from a Vegas evidence room into 'Johnny 99' and '57 Channels,' and asking 'Would Bruce ride a Honda?' He borrows Heidegger's idea that the answer already lives in the question, and uses das Man — the inauthentic 'they-self' that chooses by appearances — to contrast Harley riders who confront an existential decision with Honda's self-conserving middle-class pragmatism. The Harley as 'suicide machine' (like Captain America in Easy Rider, like Jesus's passion) embodies freedom and authenticity; Foucault's Borgesian Chinese encyclopedia reminds us that orders of things are conventional, so the ontology itself is one imaginative path among many.

holes.name: John J. McDermott
holes.what: 20th-century American philosopher of experience who built a 'metaphysics of transiency,' meliorism, and the 'Promethean self' out of James, Dewey and existentialism.
holes.why: Chapters 20 and 21 read 'Atlantic City' and 'Reason to Believe' almost entirely through McDermott's account of finitude, cutting and connecting relations, and hope without guarantees — a framework no existing taxonomy slug captures.

holes.name: Poetics (mimesis and catharsis)
holes.what: Aristotle's account of art as imitation of universal human action, in which we delight because learning pleases and poetry is more philosophic than history.
holes.why: Chapter 27 grounds its explanation of why sad story-songs like 'The River' teach and please us in the Poetics' mimesis-and-learning thesis, which none of the existing Aristotle concepts covers.
